sourceSpan.excerpt: There are versions of panpsychism that would state the following. Phenomenal states are not just extra properties of subatomic particles, they are the essence of subatomic particles. And all the other properties, like mass, charge, momentum, spin, these are all external appearances of that essence. And that comes down to a form of Leibniz-like idealism, a Monad-like theory, but that's physically incoherent. And it amazes me that this stuff is still talked about, because we have known since at least the 1940s, at least since 1949, when Feynman published his famous quantum electrodynamics paper with the Feynman diagrams and all that stuff that got the Nobel Prize, we've known since then that the particles are just metaphors for local excitations of underlying fields. In other words, there are no particles. There's nothing to a particle, but the underlying field, just as there is nothing to a ripple, but the underlying lake. You can't fish the ripple out of the lake, because the ripple is a doing of the lake. It's not a thing, it's a behavior. Particles are the same thing. Particles are behaviors of underlying quantum fields. And without this, we couldn't begin to make sense of a great many things we know happen. For instance, we couldn't make sense of particle decay. A Higgs boson can decay into two quarks or two muons, which are heavy electrons. But there aren't two muons in the Higgs boson. So how does it become two muons? Well, it's because decaying means that a particular excitation in the underlying field, in this case, the Higgs field, decays. One ripple becomes two other ripples. There is no magic in that. But if you think particles are things, then the Higgs boson magically disappears and two muons magically appear. It's like, what the hell? But I don't even need to go that far. We wouldn't be able to explain particle interactions, which is something quantum theory doesn't give us, only quantum field theory. So there are no particles, and panpsychism assumes that there are particles with delineated spatial boundaries, and that they are self-existing things. Now, this is physically contradictory. That's only one version of panpsychism. I'm not going to defend panpsychism, but I do enjoy playing around with it. But there are lots of other forms that say only living things can be conscious, or only higher order thinking things will be conscious, or different sized objects. There's all sorts of variations. Or even just representations. Maybe any system that represents something as internal or external to itself could have experience. There's lots of versions. But what I got confused with what you were saying was, I thought you were just talking about Leibniz, and then physics, and Feynman, and so on. But were you actually talking about what you believe? Because what is this underlying field? If you are an idealist, what do you mean by an underlying field? Fields, under quantum theory, are models. We model nature in terms of fields. And fields are spatially distributed. They exist in every point of spacetime. That's the model of a field. But everything in science is a convenient fiction. Like when Newton proposed this invisible force acting at a distance instantaneously between the Earth and the Moon, the force of gravity, that was a convenient fiction. Today it's no longer convenient. We know there is no such force. Gravity is a distortion of spacetime, a bending of spacetime. Actually, even that later convenient fiction is now falling by the wayside. Because now with quantum loop gravity, that whole thing is being revised. So we shouldn't take the 17 quantum fields that exist today as real existence. Because they are just conceptual models that allow us to predict nature's behavior. Now what it does tell us is that whatever is going on, it's not spatially localized. The world is not made of little bricks that are put together. That's not how nature works. Unless you make that step to fields, a great many things would break. You wouldn't be able to reconcile quantum theory with relativity. You wouldn't be able to explain particle interaction. You wouldn't be able to explain particle decay. You wouldn't be able to explain the quantum foam or spontaneous quantum excitations. And therefore you wouldn't be able to explain what people call zero point force, which is Casimir's effect, which is experimentally demonstrated. So what these models are telling us is that at the bottom level, nature is not spatially localized. That's the bottleneck. And it dovetails nicely with idealism, at least with objective forms of idealism, which say, yes, there is a world out there. It's not in our minds. It's not susceptible to our fantasy, our wishes, or our affirmations every morning. It's objective from our point of view, and it would still be there even if we were not here. But it too is mental in nature, just like my thoughts are objective from your point of view. Even if you were not there, I would still be having thoughts. And whatever fantasy you may entertain, it doesn't affect my thoughts. From your point of view, my thoughts are objective, but they are out there. They are outside your personal mind. So the claim is there are mental processes out there. They are not ours. They are objective from our perspective. They are predictable. That's why science works. They are non-localized, because there is only one field of subjectivity. This is critical to avoid the combination problem. And it dovetails nicely with field theory, because for the past 40 years, the whole of physics is trying to do the so-called grand unification theory, sort of folding gravity into the quantum fields and going from 17 to 1. And theory was an attempt, and now we have quantum gravity. So it dovetails nicely with that. But forget idealism. There are no particles. This is not my belief. This is not my opinion. This is textbook quantum field theory. It's the basis of the standard model. It's what is guiding us when we invest billions of dollars or euros at CERN. This is not even news. Some would claim we've known that since the 1920s, but at least since the 1940s.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is only one field of subjectivity
moveEvidence.claimSummary: Kastrup argues particle-based panpsychism conflicts with field theory and proposes one objective, nonlocalized field of subjectivity whose activity appears as nature.
moveEvidence.reasonSummary: Particles are excitations rather than self-existing units, while scientific fields are predictive models pointing to nonlocal underlying reality; one subjectivity also avoids the combination problem.

inferenceSummary.premise: Modern physics replaces bounded particles with field excitations and seeks unification.
inferenceSummary.inference: A many-particle consciousness ontology is ill-fitted, whereas a single nonlocalized mental field dovetails with the structure.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Objective idealism is a coherent economical interpretation of the modeled world.

burdenContact.rationale: Provides the positive one-field account and contrast with panpsychism.

moveEvidence.importanceRationale: This is the central constructive metaphysical case.

responseComponents.description: Rejects particle-based versions and subsumes essence-based versions under idealism.

moveEvidence.attributionRationale: The passage contains Kastrup’s sustained field-theoretic and idealist explanation, interrupted by Blackmore asking about other panpsychisms and the meaning of fields; those clarifications remain context, not Kastrup’s claims. His quoted statements and proposed ontology are clearly identified.
moveEvidence.materialWordingRationale: The field and subjectivity claims are repeatedly stated.
moveEvidence.spanLengthRationale: The long span is necessary because the physics argument, ontology, and combination-problem conclusion form one integrated reply.

option-a.rationale: A label covering every appearance-reality correction would lack discrimination, but Blackmore had just narrowed her target to metacognitive self-stories.

option-b.rationale: The general principle that a label applying to almost all scientific correction has little discriminating value is sound as a semantic challenge.

moveEvidence.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup

sourceSpan.excerpt: I don't totally go along with your use of the word illusionism and I don't blame you for that or anything, but I'm not comfortable with it. And the reason is the following. Defined so vaguely, the history of science is the history of illusion, because hardly anything is what it seems to be. I mean, you see, the whole history of science is a testament to that. So if the word is so broad that it encompasses so much, it becomes a useless word because we can't specify something out of the background by using it.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the history of science is the history of illusion
moveEvidence.claimSummary: Kastrup maintains that an overly broad definition of illusionism lacks discriminating content.
moveEvidence.reasonSummary: Nearly every scientific discovery shows appearances differ from reality, so that generic fact cannot identify a distinctive consciousness thesis.

inferenceSummary.premise: Almost nothing studied by science is exactly as it seems.
inferenceSummary.inference: A label applying to nearly everything specifies little.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Illusionism needs a narrower target to be useful.

burdenContact.rationale: Preserves the specificity objection after areas of agreement emerge.

responseComponents.description: Questions whether the proposed label discriminates enough even after experiential clarification.
